newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan further eases rules on China shipping.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan further eases rules on China shipping.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday announced a further easing of restrictions on shipping across the Taiwan strait, saying ships wholly owned by rival China could now make quasi-direct passage via Hong Kong or a third country.

Since February, Taiwan has quietly been allowing ships to make crossings with only a brief stop-over in Hong Kong, but has drawn the line at ships for which mainland Chinese firms owned more than a 50 percent interest.

The regulation will be relaxed to allow any mainland-owned ship to make such passages as long as it flies the flag of Hong Kong or a third country, not that of the communist People's Republic of China.
"I think there is no problem for this, since they will all fly foreign flags," Transport Minister Tsay Jaw-yang told reporters when asked about passages by China-owned ships.
A ministry official who asked not to be identified said Taiwan hoped its decision to ease the ownership restriction would prompt Beijing to lift its own ban on Taiwan-owned ships.
Taiwan's Yangming Marine Transport Corp and Uniglory Marine Corp have applied and are awaiting China's approval to began quasi-direct Taiwan-mainland routes.
Officials from Yangming and Uniglory were not available for immediate comment.

The Hong Kong-registered container ship Lien Fung, which has minority mainland ownership, was allowed to enter Taiwan's southern port of Kaohsiung on February 23 after a dog-leg voyage from China's Xiamen port via Hong Kong.
That passage, the first such quasi-direct sailing in 48 years, was the first in which a mainland cargo was delivered to Taiwan directly without having to be trans-shipped in Hong Kong.

In a separate late April development, Taiwan and China began allowing direct crossings between Kaohsiung and the mainland ports of Xiamen and Fuzhou, but Taiwan has not allowed those ships to put mainland cargoes directly into Taiwan customs.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes cannot be loaded for direct passage to China.
Taiwan business interests are keen to increase their role in the development of mainland China's economy, despite a bitter rivalry dating to a civil war split in 1949.
Taiwan still bans direct links with China and is wary of allowing Taiwan to become overdependent on its rival's economy.
